newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bond rates end higher after Australian weakness.
newsitem.headline: NZ bond rates end higher after Australian weakness.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against yesterday's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (MAR) 92.19 (PREV 92.18) 90-DAYS 7.76 (PREV 7.80)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.35 PCT (PREV 7.40) US 5-YR 6.40 (PREV 6.38)
* NZ bond yields finish higher after promising start
* Treasurer Peters seen on best behaviour for Tuesday's BPS
* Dealers see market opening a touch weaker on Tuesday
New Zealand bond yields succumbed to the Australian trend at Monday's close after a valiant attempt at a rally first thing this morning.

The mid bonds ended a basis point weaker at 7.58 percent after rallying down to 7.51 percent on the open, while the 10-year maturity closed three basis points weaker at 7.66 percent, after opening at 7.59 percent.
Dealers said the early strength had come on the back of aggressive price-making as traders scrambled to buy 7/98s, which were in short supply.
"There was a bit of demand to start the day, particularly in the July 1998s -- every man and his dog was trying to get his hands on those. That flowed out along the curve basically," one dealer said.
"But now we've had a bit of a sell-off in the Aussie (market), and someone came out and gave the '98s. The whole curve basically mirrored what happened in Australia."
The dealer said despite its best attempts the market had not transcended the bearish tone that pervaded trade last week.

"I think we'll hit 7.75 percent farily soon in the 10-years. And given that the previous range for them was 7.20 to 7.40 percent -- we were stuck there for about a month -- it's a pretty big blast out of that."

Meanwhile, money market dealers said bill rates had ended on their opening levels after being pushed lower in the interim on the back of a rate-set. Volumes had dwindled after the rate-set and were light for most of the session.

Dealers expect Tuesday's Budget Policy Statement to be a fairly routine affair. Winston Peters has taken a conservative line since he became Treasurer in a coalition deal between the National and New Zealand First parties, following October's general election, and dealers said he would probably remain on his best behaviour.
The next key statement for financial markets is the Reserve Bank's economic projections due on March 13.
